record.ear: Fair and cold. High 28. Low 17. Ice at Whitestone eleven inches.

lead.headline: Senate ratifies the Kellogg treaty 85 to 1; roll call cut on a copper master
lead.deck: Vote taken at 1:07 p.m. after two hours' debate; Senator Blaine of Wisconsin the one nay; master sealed with the instrument at 4:40 p.m.
lead.body: The Senate ratified the general treaty for the renunciation of war at 1:07 p.m. yesterday by 85 votes to 1, Senator John J. Blaine of Wisconsin voting no. The roll call was taken on the Senate's system and a copper master cut in the Capitol's recording room, which the State Department sealed with the instrument of ratification at 4:40 p.m. The master runs 6 minutes 12 seconds. Senator Borah asked that the clerk's reading of the title be included. The President is expected to sign tomorrow.

columns.headline: Hum and rate hearing adjourned to the 29th after the company's engineer answers
columns.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey adjourned the joint hearing on the Hum and the 7 1/2-cent rate to January 29 yesterday. Mr. Roland Tisch stated that the company's plant 'produces no tone at any frequency.' Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia will be heard on the 29th.

columns.headline: Judiciary Committee to report the Listening Act at noon today
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's committee will file its report on the Listening Act at noon today. The report will print the disputed word of Mr. Lucius Pell's testimony 'as each record has it,' the stenographer's 'consent' and the room's 'resent,' in parallel columns, the Senator's office says.

columns.headline: Exchange holds 17 days' spare valves; 23 failures at positions on Monday
columns.body: The Queens exchange held 17 days' spare valves last night at its present rate of failure, the supervisor reports, after 23 failures at its positions on Monday against a usual 9. Callers are asked to keep calls short. The Arcade's sleeve is 1 dollar 25. Eggs are 55 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Cyril Abbot answers the Phonautograph Society's members on record No. 23 at 8 p.m. Friday in Jamaica.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 28. War is outlawed and the weather did not hear.

lead.headline: Consent or resent? Albany prints both and lets Queens pick up the receiver
lead.deck: Harlan's committee sends the Listening Act on five to two, with the stenographer and the wall sharing a page
lead.body: The Judiciary Committee reported the Listening Act at noon, five votes to two, and printed Mr. Pell's famous word in two columns side by side. On the left, the stenographer's 'consent.' On the right, the room's 'resent.' Senator Harlan says the reader may decide. Mr. Pell says the reader may not, and that he said consent. The wall in Room 332 has filed no minority report. It is in the record already. It is the record. The Assembly fights over its own copy on Tuesday.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The Radio man gets a warmer boat and a colder reception
columns.body: Mr. Pike of the Radio Division went back off Hell Gate on Monday night in a launch with a stove in it. He heard WORS 1610 for nine seconds, he says, and then the stove went out. He would like it known that the stove went out first.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why does my call take so long to go through?'
columns.body: Sir, because there are seventeen days of spare valves at the exchange and four hundred people in Queens telling their sisters about it. Keep it short. If you must say you love her, say it once. The operator has heard it the second time and was not moved.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Kew Gardens holds a recital, and a parlour holds a grudge
columns.body: Darlings, Mrs. Grieve gave her musicale on Sunday, and the soprano sang the carol nobody can name, from memory, at the request of nobody. Mrs. Grieve left the room. The parlour, we are told, kept the whole of it. Mrs. Grieve has asked for it back.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The peace record runs six minutes twelve. The war ones ran longer.

record.ear: Cloudy and colder. High 25. Low 16. Snow flurries by evening.

lead.headline: Judiciary Committee reports the Listening Act favourably, five to two
lead.deck: Report prints Mr. Pell's disputed word in parallel columns; Senators Voight and Cassidy dissent; Assembly print set for debate Tuesday
lead.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's Judiciary Committee reported the Listening Act favourably at noon yesterday by five votes to two, Senators Voight and Cassidy dissenting. The report prints Mr. Lucius Pell's testimony of the 9th in parallel columns where the stenographer's minutes and the room's record differ, the one reading 'consent' and the other 'resent.' Mr. Pell has written to the committee that he said consent. The bill goes to the Senate calendar. The Assembly's companion print, introduced by Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt, is set for debate on Tuesday.

columns.headline: A sailor named Popeye appears in the comic pages today
columns.body: A one-eyed sailor called Popeye is introduced today in Mr. E. C. Segar's strip, Thimble Theatre, which is carried by an evening paper of Manhattan. He is engaged by Mr. Castor Oyl to crew a ship to Dice Island. Mr. Segar has not said how long he will stay.

columns.headline: Radio Division reports WORS 1610 heard nine seconds off Hell Gate
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division reports that a station giving the call WORS 1610 was received for nine seconds at 1:40 a.m. on Tuesday off Hell Gate, from the Division's launch. No bearing was taken. Mr. Pike reports that the launch's stove failed at 1:41.

columns.headline: Byrd names 42 men to winter at Little America
columns.body: Commander Byrd's message of last night, played at 10 in the Record's window, names the 42 men who will winter at Little America when the ships sail north next month. The pups remain. The temperature at the camp at noon, local time, was 18 above.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Arcade's hardware counter held 40 sleeves of valves at closing, at 1 dollar 25.

speaker.ear: Colder, flurries tonight. High 25. A sailor came in on the funnies' tide.

lead.headline: Jamaica stands on hold for valves, and the line goes dead at twenty to seven
lead.deck: Three hundred and forty in the cold outside Fogel's for a hundred and twenty sleeves; the last two hundred go home to quiet sets
lead.body: Word got round Jamaica last night that Fogel's Radio on Jamaica Avenue had a Brooklyn jobber's stock in, and by five this morning there were three hundred and forty people on the pavement. Mr. Aaron Fogel opened at six with a hundred and twenty sleeves at a dollar thirty and a limit of one. They were gone by twenty to seven. The rest went home to sets that will not last the month. He says he has never been so popular or so sorry.

columns.headline: A one-eyed sailor signs on in the funnies, and we give him our ear
columns.body: A sailor called Popeye walked into the Thimble Theatre this morning, squinting, and signed on for Dice Island. He talks out of the side of his mouth, which in Queens would get him three operators listening in. We like him. We expect he will not last.

columns.headline: Coolidge signs for peace, and the pen is quieter than the needle
columns.body: President Coolidge signed the ratification of the Kellogg treaty this afternoon. A pen makes no sound worth keeping, so the State Department recorded the room instead: a cough, a chair and a clock. The copper is sealed. The cough is now, in a manner of speaking, international law.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: an engagement in Jackson Heights goes out over the wire
columns.body: Darlings, a certain bride-to-be of 82nd Street telephoned eleven friends on Tuesday with her news, and the exchange, which has seventeen days of valves left, asked her very kindly to write to the twelfth. She did. It was the best letter of her life.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Snow tonight. The sailor in the funnies says he is used to it. He would be.

record.ear: Snow, an inch, then clearing and much colder. High 19. Low 7.

lead.headline: 340 queue from 5 a.m. at a Jamaica radio dealer for 120 sleeves of valves
lead.deck: Stock bought from a Brooklyn jobber sold out by 6:40 a.m. at 1 dollar 30, limit one; two patrolmen of the 103rd Precinct keep the pavement clear
lead.body: A line of 340 persons formed outside Fogel's Radio on Jamaica Avenue from 5 a.m. yesterday, on word that the shop had bought receiving valves from a Brooklyn jobber. Mr. Aaron Fogel opened at 6 with 120 six-sleeves at 1 dollar 30, a limit of one, and was sold out at 6:40. Two patrolmen of the 103rd Precinct kept the pavement clear for the trolley. The temperature was 21. Queens dealers held 410 sleeves at last night's close by the Record's canvass. Eggs are 55 cents.

columns.headline: President signs the ratification of the Kellogg treaty at 12:30 p.m.
columns.body: President Coolidge signed the instrument of ratification of the general treaty for the renunciation of war at 12:30 p.m. yesterday at the White House. The signing was recorded at the State Department's request and the record added to the copper master sealed on Tuesday.

columns.headline: Third parcel for the exchange cat, wrapped in an evening paper
columns.body: A third parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was delivered yesterday, postmarked Corona, January 16, and containing a tin of sardines. It was wrapped in a page of the Loud Speaker of the 12th. The supervisor reports the hand 'the same.'

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society meets at 8 tonight on record No. 23
columns.body: Members of the Phonautograph Society of Queens meet at 8 tonight at the Jamaica office to hear Mr. Cyril Abbot on record No. 23, the Maspeth party's midnight record, withheld from the 1978 case. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve's motion that it be played will be put.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Interborough reports ice forming on the Astoria line's third rail after 9 p.m.

speaker.ear: Snow, then cold enough to stop a clock. High 19. Bring the cat in.

lead.headline: Party Line gets her third tin, and the wrapping rings a bell
lead.deck: Sardines from Corona again, in the same hand, and this time wrapped in our own page of the 12th; the Speaker is reading itself very carefully
lead.body: The third tin came for Party Line yesterday, Corona postmark, same careful hand, same sardines. The supervisor unwrapped it in front of the cat and found it bundled in a page of this paper, the 12th, the one with a tall woman in a long fur coat getting off a Flushing train at Corona. It may be a coincidence. Corona reads the Speaker, three to one. The cat ate five. Sergeant Moran read the page twice, the supervisor says, and asked to keep it.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Should my boy eat his spinach?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator gives no medical advice, but she has heard a great many boys refuse spinach down the line, and she notes that the new sailor in the funnies is built like a coal barge and has not mentioned a vegetable once. We would not count on him.

columns.headline: Marchetti's room goes to a baker, and his toolbag goes to the station house
columns.body: Joseph Marchetti's landlady in Ridgewood has let his room to a baker, the warrant being weeks old and the rent older. His toolbag, pliers and a lineman's test set went to the 104th Precinct. The baker says the room hums. Every room in Queens hums. Bake louder.

columns.headline: Fogel's sells out in forty minutes, and Jamaica's sets go on short rations
columns.body: A hundred and twenty sleeves at a dollar thirty, one a head, gone by twenty to seven. Mr. Fogel says the Brooklyn man has no more. The used valve on Jackson Avenue touched fifty cents at noon. Eggs held at fifty-five. Breakfast remains a bargain.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Ice on the Astoria third rail tonight. The trains are told to go gently. The trains never listen.

record.ear: Fair and bitter cold. High 12. Low 1. The Sound freezing to Throgs Neck.

lead.headline: Society declines to play record No. 23 by 19 votes to 18; Mr. Abbot votes
lead.deck: Members' meeting sits 2 hours 40 minutes; the Maspeth party asks that the record be withheld 'for a year'; Mrs. Grieve to move again in February
lead.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens declined last night, by 19 votes to 18, to play record No. 23, the Maspeth party's midnight record, which was withheld from the 1978 case on the 8th. Mr. Cyril Abbot voted with the majority. He told the meeting that the three members of the Maspeth party had asked in writing that the record be withheld 'for a year,' and that he had agreed. He did not give their reason. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve will move again in February.

columns.headline: Week's count: 131 valve failures at the Queens exchange in seven days
columns.body: The Queens exchange recorded 131 valve failures at its positions in the seven days to last night, against 63 in an ordinary week, the supervisor reports. Spare valves on hand are 14 days' worth at that rate. Newark has not answered the exchange's request for priority.

columns.headline: Mr. Marchetti's room let; his tools held at the 104th Precinct
columns.body: The room in Ridgewood occupied until November by Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, for whom a bench warrant is outstanding, has been let, his landlady reports. A canvas bag of his tools, with a lineman's test set, is held at the 104th Precinct.

columns.headline: Cold wave to bring zero by Sunday morning, Weather Bureau says
columns.body: The Weather Bureau gives zero or below in the city by Sunday morning, with northwest winds to 30 miles. The Health Department asks that coal be ordered today. The Bowery Bay Ice Company will cut at Whitestone and Willets Point through the weekend.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Interborough reports four delays on the Astoria line from ice on the third rail between 6 and 9 p.m.

speaker.ear: Bitter. High 12. Zero by morning. Your breath will be on the record.

lead.headline: Society votes to keep Maspeth on hold, and Abbot finally picks up
lead.deck: Nineteen to eighteen against hearing record No. 23; the man who would not vote on a carol votes on this one; Mrs. Grieve promises February
lead.body: Last night the Phonautograph Society decided, by one vote, not to hear its own midnight. The vote was Mr. Abbot's. He sat out the carol fight in a chair at the back, and last night he walked to the front to vote no. The three Maspeth men, he said, had asked in writing for their record to rest a year, and he had agreed. Why? He did not say. Mrs. Grieve said February. She said it twice, so the room would have it. The Society adjourned to cocoa.

columns.headline: Byrd's winter list is forty-two names long, and the dogs don't count
columns.body: Commander Byrd has named the forty-two men who will stay on the Barrier when the ships go north. The pups are staying too, Jackson among them, but the Navy does not count dogs. The men will be on the air nightly. The dogs will be on it anyway.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A Woodside milkman picks it up on his early round
columns.body: A Woodside milkman says WORS 1610 came up on the set in his stable at four on Friday morning, very faint, while he was harnessing. His horse stood still for the whole of it, which the horse has never done. He did not record it. The horse, he says, remembers.

columns.headline: Fourteen days of spares, and the operators get short with everybody
columns.body: The exchange broke a hundred and thirty-one valves this week and has fourteen days of spares left. Newark is still 'considering.' The supervisor asks callers to keep it brief. One operator asks callers to keep it interesting, if they cannot keep it brief.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Zero tonight. The third rail is sulking. Walk if you can and wrap up if you cannot.

editorial.headline: Judges must be safe on dance floors
editorial.body: Judge Ambrose Teague of the Magistrates' Court, who sent thirty-two girls to the Bedford reformatory last year for the crime of being found in a dance hall without a chaperone, was himself found in a dance hall without a chaperone on Saturday, tangoing with a lady in black. She asked him what makes a girl wayward. He told her, at length, and the hall's system, which records every word spoken under its chandeliers, heard him, and so has half the borough. 'A girl alone is a girl asking,' His Honour said, and other things we will not print. This paper defends the judiciary. A judge off the bench is entitled to his opinions. We merely ask why his opinions are so much better dressed than his judgments.

record.ear: Clear and bitter. High 8. Low 2 below at 6 a.m. Sound frozen to Throgs Neck.

lead.headline: Steinway church cannot broadcast its service today for want of one valve
lead.deck: First Reformed Church's output valve failed Thursday; Newark makes the only replacement; 212 shut-ins without the service for the first Sunday since 1907
lead.body: The First Reformed Church of Steinway will not broadcast its morning service today, its transmitter's output valve having failed on Thursday evening, the Rev. Martin Ostrander announced. The valve, a fifty-watt type made only at the Newark works, cannot be had. The church has broadcast every Sunday since 1907 under its licence for shut-ins, of whom 212 are on its list. Mr. Ostrander has asked members with telephones to call one shut-in each after the service and read them the sermon, printed for the purpose.

columns.headline: Byrd's party completes winter quarters; ships to sail by mid-February
columns.body: Commander Byrd's message of last night reports the winter quarters at Little America completed, with a radio house, a machine shop and a mess hall under the snow and joined by tunnels. The City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling will sail by mid-February.

columns.headline: Ice companies cut through the night on the Sound; 3,800 tons housed Saturday
columns.body: The Bowery Bay and Whitestone ice companies cut by lantern through Friday night and housed 3,800 tons on Saturday, the largest day's cutting of the season. The Willets Point field reopened at 13 inches. Mr. Owen Pratt says 'one more week like this and Queens has a summer.'

columns.headline: Health Department warns against banked coal fires in closed rooms
columns.body: The Health Department asks householders not to keep coal fires banked in closed rooms overnight, after two deaths from fumes in Brooklyn on Friday. Coal is 15 dollars the ton. The Long Island City yards report deliveries delayed by ice on the hills.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Interborough reports 19 delays on the Astoria and Flushing lines from ice on the third rail between 6 p.m. and midnight.

speaker.ear: Two below at six. The Sound is solid. So is everyone's resolve to stay in bed.

lead.headline: Steinway church loses its broadcast, and the faithful pass the receiver
lead.deck: One dead valve silences a Sunday that has gone out over the air since 1907; the pastor's answer is the telephone and two hundred good neighbours
lead.body: For twenty-two years the First Reformed Church of Steinway has sent its Sunday service over the air to the sick and the snowed-in. This morning it cannot. One fifty-watt valve gave out on Thursday, and the only place that makes them is a burnt glass shop in Newark. So Mr. Ostrander has printed his sermon and asked every member with a telephone to ring one shut-in after church and read it down the line. The operators say they will not listen. They will, a little.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring the church?'
columns.body: Madam, you can ring the church, and the church will answer, but it cannot ring you back today, its valve being dead. After eleven, two hundred of its members will be ringing two hundred shut-ins with the sermon. Please do not ring anyone else before one.

columns.headline: Byrd's men move under the snow, and the tunnels carry the line
columns.body: Little America's winter quarters are done: a radio house, a machine shop and a mess hall, all under the snow and joined by tunnels, so nobody need go outside to talk. In Queens we call that a basement flat. The ships go north in February.

columns.headline: Ice men cut by lantern, and the Sound takes a close shave
columns.body: Bowery Bay cut all Friday night by lantern and housed thirty-eight hundred tons on Saturday, the best day of the winter. Willets Point is open at thirteen inches. Mr. Pratt was seen smiling, and his men have asked for a record of it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Nineteen delays on the elevated last night. The third rail has gone on strike and wants more coal.

record.ear: Clear and cold. High 14. Low 3. Coldest January Sunday since 1918.

lead.headline: Ice on the third rail stalls an Astoria train 47 minutes at Queensboro Plaza
lead.deck: Two below zero at 6 a.m. Sunday; 31 delays on the Astoria and Flushing lines; Interborough runs sleet cars all night
lead.body: The thermometer at the Weather Bureau read two below zero at 6 a.m. yesterday, the coldest January Sunday since 1918. At 7:12 p.m. an Astoria train lost its contact shoe to ice on the third rail at the Queensboro Plaza curve and stood 47 minutes, with 340 passengers aboard, until a sleet car cleared the rail. The Interborough reports 31 delays on the Astoria and Flushing lines between 6 p.m. and 2 a.m. Guards report the rail 'silent,' which they said is unusual.

columns.headline: Steinway service read by telephone to 197 shut-ins
columns.body: Members of the First Reformed Church of Steinway read the Rev. Martin Ostrander's printed sermon by telephone to 197 of the church's 212 shut-ins yesterday between noon and 3 p.m., the Queens exchange reports. Fifteen could not be reached. The church's valve remains unobtainable.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five beat the Paterson Crescents 33 to 24
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club five beat the Paterson Crescents 33 to 24 at the armory on Saturday night before 700, the armory's heating having been restored. Mr. Frank Dillon scored 14. The club stands at seven wins and five losses.

columns.headline: Kissena Lake hockey: Flushing seven beat Jamaica 4 to 1
columns.body: The Flushing seven beat Jamaica 4 to 1 on Kissena Lake yesterday afternoon at two below zero before 600. The referee's whistle froze in the second period and play was stopped by hand-bell thereafter. The ice measured eleven inches.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Assembly takes up Assemblyman Burkhardt's print of the Listening Act at 11 a.m. tomorrow.

speaker.ear: Cold enough to crack a bell. High 14. The elevated is staying in.

lead.headline: Third rail freezes, and an Astoria train is left on hold for 47 minutes
lead.deck: Two below at six, a shoe off at the Plaza curve, and three hundred and forty people learn what the elevated sounds like when it stops
lead.body: At twelve past seven last night an Astoria train hit the Plaza curve, lost its shoe to the ice on the third rail and sat there. Forty-seven minutes. Three hundred and forty people with their feet in their hats. A sleet car came at last and scraped the rail clean, and the train went on, grumbling. A guard told us the rail had gone silent, which he said was the worst of it. That rail has sizzled politely for twenty years. Last night it had nothing to say.

columns.headline: Steinway's sermon goes out on two hundred lines, and the house is full
columns.body: The First Reformed Church read its sermon by telephone to a hundred and ninety-seven shut-ins yesterday, two hundred members ringing between noon and three. Fifteen did not answer. One old gentleman asked to hear the second half again, which no Sunday in history has ever produced.

columns.headline: Club five warm up the armory and leave Paterson out in the cold
columns.body: The heat was back on at the armory, and the Athletic Club five beat the Paterson Crescents 33 to 24 in shirtsleeves. Dillon scored fourteen. Seven won, five lost. The seven hundred in the stands had their coats off by half time and back on for the walk home.

columns.headline: Kissena hockey whistle freezes, and the ref switches to a bell
columns.body: The referee's whistle froze to his lip in the second period of Flushing's 4 to 1 win over Jamaica, and he finished the game ringing a hand-bell. Players said it was the first time they had ever been rung off. Six hundred watched, stamping.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Assembly argues the Listening Act tomorrow. The galleries are recording. The Assembly is recording the galleries.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 20. Low 9. Moderating by Thursday.

lead.headline: Retired motorman's parlour record played at his funeral, at his request
lead.deck: Mr. Cornelius Byrne, 81, drove trains on the elevated 41 years; nine minutes of a Sunday evening in his Woodside parlour played before the coffin; burial at Mount Olivet
lead.body: Mr. Cornelius Byrne, who drove trains on the elevated for 41 years and retired in 1919, was buried yesterday at Mount Olivet Cemetery, Maspeth, after a service at the Duffy funeral parlour on Roosevelt Avenue. He was 81, and died on Thursday. At his written request, nine minutes of his parlour's record of a Sunday evening in 1926 were played before the coffin to 140 mourners. It contains a game of pinochle and his voice disputing a trick. His daughter, Mrs. Agnes Toomey, said 'he won it, too.'

columns.headline: Assembly to debate the Listening Act at 11 today; amendment expected
columns.body: The Assembly takes up Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt's print of the Listening Act at 11 this morning. Assemblyman Dennis Kilbride of Kings has given notice of an amendment requiring 'the consent of the occupant' before any room's record is admitted in evidence.

columns.headline: Valves 1 dollar 35 at the Arcade; exchange spares at 13 days
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's hardware counter priced the sleeve of receiving valves at 1 dollar 35 yesterday, with 26 in stock. The Queens exchange reports 13 days' spares. Used valves were 55 cents on Jackson Avenue. Eggs are 54 cents, butter 56.

columns.headline: Interborough reports 12 delays from third-rail ice on Monday night
columns.body: Sleet cars ran on the Astoria and Flushing lines from 5 p.m. to 3 a.m., the Interborough reports, and delays from ice on the third rail fell to 12 from Sunday night's 31. No train stood longer than nine minutes.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'calm, 22 above, all hands busy' at 9:55 p.m.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 20. The Assembly is the warmest room in the State today.

lead.headline: Assembly gets its wires crossed on 'consent,' and the gallery throws a spark
lead.deck: Four hours of shouting over the Listening Act; Kilbride's 'consent of the occupant' goes down by five; the bill limps on to third reading
lead.body: The Assembly opened on the Listening Act at eleven and was still at it at three, all of it on the chamber's own system, which nobody moved to switch off this time, having heard how that goes. Mr. Kilbride of Brooklyn wanted no room's record in court without the occupant's consent. Mr. Burkhardt of Queens said a dead man cannot consent and a burgled one should not have to. Somebody in the gallery said 'resent.' The amendment lost seventy-four to sixty-nine, and the bill went on.

columns.headline: Old motorman makes his last run with a winning hand on the record
columns.body: Cornelius Byrne drove the elevated for forty-one years and asked to be sent off with nine minutes of a Sunday at home: pinochle, a kettle, and himself disputing a trick. They played it at Duffy's yesterday. A hundred and forty mourners laughed. His daughter says he won the trick.

columns.headline: Valves at a dollar thirty-five, and the exchange counts down on its fingers
columns.body: Thirteen days of spares at the exchange, twenty-six sleeves at the Arcade at a dollar thirty-five, and the used valve at fifty-five cents. Eggs are fifty-four. If this goes on, the pawnbroker will be wearing a valve on his watch chain.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is the third rail fixed?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator does not run the elevated. She rides it, like you, and last night she stood at the Plaza nine minutes with a sleet car scraping ahead of her. The rail is not fixed. It is merely scraped. So is she.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Kilbride lost by five. He says the five did not consent. They say they resent that.

record.ear: Fair, less cold. High 24. Low 15. Ice cutting continues on the Sound.

lead.headline: Assembly rejects 'consent of the occupant' amendment, 74 to 69
lead.deck: Debate on the Listening Act runs 4 hours 12 minutes; bill ordered to third reading; a voice from the gallery at 2:51 p.m. not identified
lead.body: The Assembly yesterday rejected, 74 to 69, Assemblyman Dennis Kilbride's amendment to the Listening Act requiring the consent of the occupant before a room's record is admitted in evidence, and ordered Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt's print to a third reading. The debate ran 4 hours 12 minutes and was taken on the chamber's own system. At 2:51 p.m. a voice from the public gallery said the word 'resent.' Speaker McGinnies ordered the gallery cleared for ten minutes. The voice has not been identified from the record.

columns.headline: Assembly debate, from the chamber's record, 1:40 p.m.
columns.body: MR. KILBRIDE: 'A man's parlour is his own. Must it go to court without him?' MR. BURKHARDT: 'If he is dead, it is all that can go. On Monday a parlour spoke at a funeral, and nobody asked it to consent.' MR. KILBRIDE: 'He asked it.'

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin to measure the Hum at 23 places before the 29th
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia will take readings of the Hum at 23 places in Queens between today and Friday, at Alderman Feeney's request, for the Public Service Commission's hearing on the 29th. Queens Light & Power has declined to admit him to its Astoria works.

columns.headline: Ice companies house 21,000 tons in a week; harvest at 52,200
columns.body: The three Sound ice companies housed 21,000 tons in the seven days to last night, the Bowery Bay company reports, bringing the season's harvest to 52,200 tons. Mr. Owen Pratt says the houses will be full by February 5 'if the cold stays.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Saul Feder has filed the record of the Assembly debate as an exhibit to his motion in the Lasko case.

speaker.ear: Less cold. High 24. The ice houses are filling and the ice men are full of themselves.

lead.headline: Albany plays back the gallery, and the heckler keeps his number unlisted
lead.deck: Ten minutes of cleared gallery, four hours of debate, and one word from the cheap seats that nobody will own
lead.body: At nine minutes to three yesterday, in the middle of Mr. Kilbride's last appeal, a voice from the Assembly gallery said 'resent,' clear as a bell, and Speaker McGinnies had the gallery cleared for ten minutes. Then they played the chamber's record back to find the culprit. It has the word. It has the voice. It has no face, being a record. Ninety people were up there. All ninety say it was somebody else. Mr. Pell, we are assured, was in New York at the time.

columns.headline: Rastin takes his meter round Queens, and the company keeps him off the line
columns.body: Dr. Rastin of Columbia will read the hum at twenty-three places in Queens this week for Alderman Feeney. Queens Light & Power will not let him into its Astoria works. He says he will stand at the gate. The gate, we expect, will hum.

columns.headline: Lasko's lawyer files Albany's argument, and the case gets a longer cord
columns.body: Mr. Feder has filed the record of yesterday's Assembly debate as proof that nobody in Albany agrees, which is the one thing everybody in Albany agrees on. Trial is February 18. The fur coat is not under anything we know of.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A Kew Gardens kitchen catches it between the eggs and the toast
columns.body: A cook-general in Kew Gardens writes that WORS 1610 came up on her kitchen set at half past six on Monday morning, between the eggs and the toast, with a man reading numbers. She burnt the toast. Her employer has asked that the set be kept to the parlour.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Seventy-four to sixty-nine. In Queens that is a pinochle score. In Albany it is very nearly the law.

record.ear: Cloudy, moderating. High 30. Low 21. Snow possible Friday.

lead.headline: Exchange asks callers to keep calls to three minutes; spares at 11 days
lead.deck: Supervisor's request read at every position from 7 a.m.; 29 valve failures on Tuesday; Newark to release salvaged stores 'to telephone exchanges first'
lead.body: The supervisor of the Queens exchange instructed operators from 7 a.m. yesterday to ask every caller to keep calls to three minutes, the exchange holding 11 days' spare valves after 29 failures on Tuesday. The request is read once, at connection. The Newark works wired last night that stores salvaged from the fire, about 2,000 sleeves, will be released 'to telephone exchanges first, then signals, then the trade,' beginning Monday. The Interborough protested. Calls on the Queens exchange yesterday averaged 3 minutes 40 seconds.

columns.headline: Little America plans a flight eastward 'at the first clear day'
columns.body: Commander Byrd's message of last night reports the expedition's Fairchild monoplane assembled and tested, and a flight eastward along the Barrier planned 'at the first clear day.' The message was played at 10 in the Record's window to 300, in 26 degrees.

columns.headline: Queens Light & Power refuses Dr. Rastin at the Astoria works gate
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia made a reading at the gate of the Queens Light & Power works in Astoria at 10:40 a.m. yesterday, having been refused admission. His meter read 41 cycles. A company guard stood beside him for the reading.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society to record the Borough President's dinner Saturday
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens will record the Chamber of Commerce dinner for the Borough President at the Jamaica Arms on Saturday evening, at the Chamber's invitation, for the 1978 case. Mr. Cyril Abbot says the speeches will be taken 'whole, with the soup.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The average call on the Queens exchange yesterday ran 3 minutes 40 seconds against the requested three.

speaker.ear: Milder. High 30. Snow tomorrow, maybe. Say it in three minutes.

lead.headline: Three minutes, please: the exchange puts Queens on a short line
lead.deck: Eleven days of valves left and the operators ask every caller to hurry; the borough averages three minutes forty and is not sorry
lead.body: From seven yesterday morning every caller in Queens heard a new thing before the old thing: three minutes, please. The exchange has eleven days of valves. Newark says it will send its salvage to the telephones first from Monday, and the elevated says that is all very well for people who do not need to get anywhere. The borough's average call came to three minutes and forty seconds. That is forty seconds of goodbye. You cannot hurry a Queens goodbye. Nobody has ever tried twice.

columns.headline: Rastin reads the gate, and the gate reads forty-one
columns.body: Queens Light & Power would not let Dr. Rastin in, so he stood in the street and held his meter up to the works' gate. Forty-one. A company guard stood beside him to see he did nothing, and stood in the forty-one with him, buttoned up and saying nothing.

columns.headline: Society to bottle the Borough President's dinner, soup and all
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society will record Saturday's dinner for the Borough President at the Jamaica Arms, speeches whole and with the soup, for 1978. We hope 1978 likes consomme. We hope it likes the speeches. One of those hopes is better founded.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a three-minute romance on the Astoria exchange
columns.body: Darlings, a young gentleman of Ditmars Boulevard proposed by telephone at 8:02 last night and was told 'three minutes, please' by the operator before the lady could answer. He began again, faster. She accepted at 8:04 and fifty seconds. The operator has asked to be a bridesmaid.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Newark sends its valves to the telephones first. The elevated sends its regrets, slowly.

record.ear: Snow, two inches, then clearing. High 31. Low 22.

lead.headline: Second lien notice fixed to the Arcade with brass screws; gone by morning
lead.deck: Mr. Haas replaces the notice at 3:20 p.m. Wednesday; screw holes found filled with putty at 7 a.m.; Signal Ground Rents Inc. not reached
lead.body: Mr. Ludwig Haas fixed a second notice of lien for 28 dollars to the north door of the Vantry Arcade at 3:20 p.m. on Wednesday, with four brass screws. At 7 a.m. yesterday the notice and screws were gone and the holes had been filled with putty and painted to match the door. The Arcade's eleven tenants say they saw nothing. The telephone of Signal Ground Rents Inc. was rung three times without reply. A copy is filed with the County Clerk.

columns.headline: Alderman Feeney gives notice of a fifth witness, a wire-haired terrier
columns.body: Alderman Feeney has notified the Public Service Commission that a fifth witness for the Astoria petitioners, a wire-haired terrier named Duke, owned by Mr. Anton Vrabel of 31st Street, will attend on the 29th. Mr. Vrabel states the dog 'howls at the Hum and at nothing else.'

columns.headline: Judge Conklin to rule on the Lasko record motion before trial
columns.body: Judge Conklin said yesterday he will rule on Mr. Saul Feder's motion to exclude the Hale parlour record 'before the jury is drawn' on February 18. Mr. Feder's exhibits now include the records of the Albany hearing and the Assembly debate. The fur coat has not been found.

columns.headline: Interborough to share Newark salvage valves with the exchange
columns.body: The Interborough and the Queens exchange agreed yesterday to divide the Newark works' salvaged stores two to one in the exchange's favour, the supervisor reports. The first motor truck leaves Newark on Monday at 6 a.m. Used valves were 60 cents on Jackson Avenue. Eggs are 54 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Commander Byrd reports 'clear, calm' at Little America and the Fairchild fuelled.

speaker.ear: Snow, two inches, then clear. High 31. The dogs of Astoria have been notified.

lead.headline: Astoria terrier subpoenaed over the Hum, and he's pitch perfect
lead.deck: Feeney's fifth witness is a wire-haired dog named Duke who howls at forty-one cycles and nothing else; the company is said to be seeking counsel for the defence
lead.body: Duke is four, wire-haired, and lives with Mr. Anton Vrabel on 31st Street in Astoria. He does not howl at the milkman, the coal horse, the elevated or Mrs. Vrabel's sister. He howls at the hum, and has since September, a long low note that Mr. Vrabel swears is the hum's own. Alderman Feeney has called him as a witness on Tuesday. Queens Light & Power says it makes no tone. Duke says otherwise, at length. He will be the first witness ever told to sit.

columns.headline: Lien notice goes up with brass screws and comes down with good manners
columns.body: Mr. Haas screwed his second lien notice to the Arcade door on Wednesday afternoon with four brass screws. By morning the notice was gone, the holes were puttied, and the paint matched. Whoever is ignoring the Borough is very tidy about it.

columns.headline: The judge will rule on the parlour before the jury gets an earful
columns.body: Judge Conklin says he will rule on whether the Hale parlour may testify before the jury is drawn on February 18. Mr. Feder has filed Albany's arguments in a stack. The spaniel's evidence runs two hours ten minutes. The stack is longer.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who gets the Newark valves first?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator does, two parts in three, and the elevated gets the third. You get them after, at a price that will make you fond of a dollar thirty-five. Until then, three minutes, please. Your sister already knows.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Duke's counsel says his client will not answer questions about cats.

record.ear: Fair, milder. High 33. Low 24. Thaw by Monday, the Bureau says.

lead.headline: Week's count: 22 Queens dealers hold 190 sleeves of valves at 1 dollar 45
lead.deck: Stocks lowest since the Newark fire; three dealers report none; used valves 65 cents; first salvage shipment Monday
lead.body: Twenty-two Queens hardware and radio dealers held 190 six-sleeves of receiving valves at last night's close, by the Record's canvass, against 1,060 a fortnight ago and 410 on the 17th. Three dealers, in Ozone Park, Corona and Bayside, have none. The common price is 1 dollar 45, limit one. Used valves were 65 cents on Jackson Avenue. The exchange holds 10 days' spares. The first motor truck of salvaged stores leaves Newark on Monday at 6 a.m. Eggs are 53 cents, butter 55.

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin completes readings at 23 places; results to the Commission Monday
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia completed his readings of the Hum at 23 places in Queens yesterday at 4:10 p.m., the last at the Hell Gate end of Astoria Park. His results will be filed with the Public Service Commission on Monday and heard on Tuesday.

columns.headline: Chamber of Commerce dines the Borough President tonight at the Jamaica Arms
columns.body: The Queens Chamber of Commerce gives its annual dinner for the Borough President at 7:30 tonight at the Jamaica Arms, 600 covers. The Phonautograph Society will record the speeches. Alderman Feeney has asked to speak on the Hum and has been placed ninth.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand asks to keep the first Woodside carol record until Easter
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand of Union Seminary has asked the Phonautograph Society to let him keep the first Woodside record of the carol heard on WORS 1610 until Easter. He has compared it with a further 900 tunes from the Seminary's collection without a match.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Queens exchange reports the average call yesterday at 3 minutes 22 seconds.

speaker.ear: Milder. High 33. A thaw on Monday, and the ice men are taking it personally.

lead.headline: Queens down to its last sleeves, and the borough turns down the volume
lead.deck: Three shops bare, the rest at a dollar forty-five, and a whole borough learning to switch on only when somebody important is talking
lead.body: There are a hundred and ninety sleeves of valves left in the shops of Queens, and three shops with none at all. The price is a dollar forty-five, limit one, and a used valve is sixty-five cents, which is more than a good lunch. So Queens has turned its sets down and off. The Little America hour still draws a crowd at the Record's window, because the Record pays for its own valves. Families are knitting. Families are talking. Some families are finding they did not miss it.

columns.headline: Rastin takes the borough's pitch at twenty-three corners
columns.body: Dr. Rastin finished his twenty-three readings at ten past four yesterday at the Hell Gate end of Astoria Park, with his overcoat buttoned to the chin. He will not tell us the numbers until Tuesday. He did not need to. He was humming.

columns.headline: Society to record tonight's dinner, and Feeney is ninth on the bill of fare
columns.body: Six hundred will dine the Borough President at the Jamaica Arms, and the Phonautograph Society will take it all down for 1978. Alderman Feeney has asked to speak on the hum and has been put ninth, after the fish. Ninth is where they put things they hope will go cold.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Kew Gardens knits for the Pole, and Mrs. Grieve casts off
columns.body: Darlings, the ladies of Kew Gardens have knitted forty-two mufflers for Commander Byrd's winter party, one a man, to go south when there is a ship to take them. Mrs. Grieve did six. She says she would have done more if her parlour were quieter.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Three minutes twenty-two. Queens is learning. Queens resents it.

editorial.headline: Fire department told to hose her off the courthouse
editorial.body: In the January thaw on Wednesday night a figure in black was seen walking up the face of the Long Island City courthouse as calmly as a lady climbs the stairs at Altman's, a silk cape opening behind her like an umbrella. The Fire Department was called and declined to turn its hoses on what the captain called 'a lady on a lawful errand,' namely, delivering to the clerk's window on the fourth floor the files of seven women whose divorce petitions had been 'mislaid' for two years. We demand a ladder, a hose and an explanation. Our stenographer reminds us that Lilith is spelled with one L at the end, not two. We thank Miss Penrose and dock her an hour.

record.ear: Fair and milder. High 36. Low 27. Thaw beginning.

lead.headline: Six hundred dine the Borough President at the Jamaica Arms
lead.deck: Chamber of Commerce dinner runs until 12:40 a.m.; sewers pledged for Bayside and Ozone Park; Alderman Feeney speaks ninth, on the Hum
lead.body: The Queens Chamber of Commerce gave its annual dinner for the Borough President last night at the Jamaica Arms to 600 guests, the speeches continuing until 12:40 a.m. The Borough President pledged sewers for Bayside and Ozone Park within the year and a new bridge at Flushing Creek. Alderman Feeney, speaking ninth, asked the room to be silent for one minute 'and listen.' The room was silent. The Phonautograph Society recorded the minute with the speeches. The Borough President did not refer to it.

columns.headline: Alderman Feeney at the dinner, from the Society's record, 11:48 p.m.
columns.body: ALDERMAN FEENEY: 'I ask this room for one minute of silence. Not for the dead. For the living, so you may hear what Astoria hears.' (Silence, 1 minute 2 seconds.) ALDERMAN FEENEY: 'Thank you. That is the Hum. Good night.'

columns.headline: Thaw expected Monday; ice companies cut through Sunday
columns.body: The Weather Bureau gives temperatures above freezing from Monday and rain by Wednesday. The three Sound ice companies will cut through today, a Sunday, by permission of the Police Department, the Bowery Bay company having 56,000 tons housed. Kissena Lake closes to skaters tonight.

columns.headline: Steinway church to read its sermon by telephone a second Sunday
columns.body: The Rev. Martin Ostrander of the First Reformed Church of Steinway says members will read today's sermon by telephone to the church's shut-ins for a second Sunday. The church has applied to the Newark works for one fifty-watt output valve and is ninth on the list.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'clear, the Fairchild away eastward' at 9:40 p.m.

speaker.ear: Milder at last. High 36. Six hundred stomachs in Jamaica are on the mend.

lead.headline: Feeney asks six hundred diners to hold the line, and the Hum takes the floor
lead.deck: Sewers for Bayside, a bridge for Flushing, and then the Alderman from Astoria asks for one minute of quiet after the fish
lead.body: The Chamber of Commerce dined the Borough President last night at the Jamaica Arms, six hundred of them, and the Borough President promised sewers to Bayside and a bridge to Flushing, and was cheered. Then Alderman Feeney stood up ninth and asked for one minute's silence, 'not for the dead, for the living.' Six hundred forks went down. For sixty-two seconds the Jamaica Arms heard what Astoria hears. Then the Alderman said 'that is the Hum,' sat down, and ate his dessert. Nobody else had any appetite.

columns.headline: Steinway's pulpit stays on the telephone, ninth in line for a voice
columns.body: The First Reformed Church reads its sermon down two hundred telephones again today and is ninth on Newark's list for one valve. Ninth is a bad number this week. The shut-ins say they like the telephone better. The pastor says he has heard that before.

columns.headline: Thaw on the line for Monday, and the ice men hurry to hang up
columns.body: Above freezing Monday and rain by Wednesday, says the Weather Bureau, so the ice men are cutting today, Sunday or no, with the Police Department's blessing and the Lord's toleration. Fifty-six thousand tons are in. Kissena closes tonight. Skate while you can.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What did the Borough President eat?'
columns.body: Sir, oysters, consomme, a sole, a chicken and an ice, and the Phonautograph Society has the soup on the record for 1978. The operator was not invited. She connected eleven calls from the cloakroom asking wives to wait up, and five asking them not to.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's plane went east today. The Commander will tell us what he found when he has found out what it is.

record.ear: Cloudy, above freezing. High 38. Low 30. Rain by Wednesday.

lead.headline: Byrd's party sights a range of mountains east of Little America
lead.deck: Fairchild monoplane flies some five hours along the Barrier; peaks on no chart; Commander names them for Mr. John D. Rockefeller Jr.
lead.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd reported by wire at 9:40 p.m. yesterday that the expedition's Fairchild monoplane, flying east along the Barrier from Little America, sighted a range of mountains on no chart. The flight lasted some five hours. The Commander has named the range for Mr. John D. Rockefeller Jr. The message, played twice in the Record's window to 900 persons, included eleven seconds recorded aboard the aeroplane as the peaks came into view. It contains the engine and a voice saying 'There.'

columns.headline: Athletic Club five beat the Camden Bulldogs 30 to 27 in an extra period
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club five beat the Camden Bulldogs 30 to 27 in an extra period at the armory on Saturday night before 1,100. Mr. Frank Dillon scored 11. The club stands at eight wins and five losses.

columns.headline: Kid Sorrentino stops Al Venn in the sixth at Ridgewood Grove
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino of Astoria stopped Al Venn of Philadelphia in the sixth round at Ridgewood Grove on Saturday night before 3,100. The referee's count was recorded and played to the house. Mr. Harry Lusk's manager, present, renewed his request for the seventh round of the earlier bout.

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin's readings to be filed this morning; hearing tomorrow at 10
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia will file his readings of the Hum at 23 places in Queens with the Public Service Commission this morning. The Commission resumes the joint hearing on the Hum and the 7 1/2-cent rate at 10 tomorrow. Commissioner Lacey presides.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The first motor truck of Newark salvage valves left at 6:10 a.m. with 640 sleeves, 430 for the Queens exchange.

speaker.ear: Above freezing. High 38. The ice men are listening for the drip.

lead.headline: Byrd tunes in a whole new range, and the mountains come in loud and clear
lead.deck: Some five hours east of Little America, peaks on no chart; the Commander names them for Mr. Rockefeller and sends home eleven seconds of the view
lead.body: Commander Byrd's Fairchild flew east along the Barrier on Sunday, local time, and found a whole range of mountains that no man had ever seen or charted. The Commander has named them for Mr. Rockefeller, who helped pay for the trip, which is how mountains get named. Nine hundred people on Jackson Avenue heard the eleven seconds recorded aboard as the peaks came up: an engine, and a voice saying one word. It was 'There.' There is no better word for it. We have looked.

columns.headline: Club five beat Camden in overtime, and the armory stays on the line
columns.body: The Athletic Club five and the Camden Bulldogs were level at the end, so they played on, and the club won 30 to 27 before eleven hundred people who had forgotten their trains. Dillon scored eleven. Eight won, five lost. Camden says the clock was fast.

columns.headline: Sorrentino stops Venn in six, and the count goes on the record
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino put Al Venn of Philadelphia down in the sixth at Ridgewood Grove, and the count was played back to the house so nobody could say ten was nine. Three thousand one hundred cheered twice. Lusk's manager still wants round seven of the old fight.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The Speaker starts a map, and the map starts at Hell Gate
columns.body: Readers have sent us forty-one sightings of WORS 1610 since November, and we are pinning them to a map of Queens on the office wall. Hell Gate has six pins. Maspeth has five. Woodside has a milkman's horse. We will print the map in February.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Six hundred and forty sleeves left Newark at ten past six. The exchange got four hundred and thirty, and said thank you in under three minutes.

record.ear: Cloudy, mild. High 41. Low 33. Rain tomorrow.

lead.headline: Dr. Rastin's readings find 41 cycles at all 23 places in Queens
lead.deck: Survey filed with the Commission at 9:40 a.m. yesterday; places from Hell Gate to Far Rockaway; strongest at Astoria, weakest at Bayside
lead.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia filed with the Public Service Commission yesterday his readings of the Hum, taken at 23 places in Queens between the 23rd and the 25th. The meter read 41 cycles at every place, from the Hell Gate end of Astoria Park to the boardwalk at Far Rockaway. The tone was strongest at Astoria and weakest at Bayside. Queens Light & Power, in a statement of four lines, said the readings 'do not concern the company.' The hearing resumes at 10 today.

columns.headline: Salvaged valves reach the Queens exchange; spares restored to 19 days
columns.body: The Queens exchange received 430 six-sleeves of salvaged valves from the Newark works at 11:20 a.m. yesterday, restoring its spares to 19 days, the supervisor reports. The three-minute request will continue 'for the present.' The Interborough received 210 sleeves. None reached the trade.

columns.headline: Second Steinway Sunday by telephone reaches 204 shut-ins
columns.body: Members of the First Reformed Church of Steinway read the Rev. Martin Ostrander's sermon by telephone to 204 of the church's 212 shut-ins on Sunday, the exchange reports, against 197 a week earlier. The church remains ninth on the Newark works' list.

columns.headline: Society's record of the Chamber dinner to go into the fourth copper case
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society's record of Saturday's Chamber of Commerce dinner, 4 hours 50 minutes on nine masters, will go into the fourth copper case for 1978, Mr. Cyril Abbot says, including Alderman Feeney's silence of 62 seconds.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Anton Vrabel confirms that the terrier Duke will attend the Commission at 10 today, on a lead.

speaker.ear: Mild and grey. High 41. Forty-one, like everything else this week.

lead.headline: Duke takes the stand, hits the note, and company counsel is howled down
lead.deck: Rastin's twenty-three forty-ones read into the record; the terrier howls on cue in a silent room; Commissioner Lacey reserves on the Hum and the half cent alike
lead.body: At a quarter past eleven, Dr. Rastin having read his twenty-three forty-ones into the record, Alderman Feeney asked the Commission for a minute's quiet. In it, Duke of 31st Street lifted his head and howled, one long low note, and Dr. Rastin's meter said forty-one. Company counsel objected that a dog is not an instrument. Commissioner Lacey said he had noticed. Mr. Tisch said the company makes no tone. Duke said nothing further. The Commissioner reserved decision on both the hum and the rate, to February.

columns.headline: Salvage valves reach the exchange, and the operators get some slack in the line
columns.body: Four hundred and thirty sleeves came off the Newark truck at the exchange yesterday, and the spares are back to nineteen days. The three-minute request stays. The shops got none. Used valves are sixty cents, and the pawnbroker has started polishing them.

columns.headline: Two hundred and four hear Steinway's sermon, and the line is the new pulpit
columns.body: Two hundred and four of the church's two hundred and twelve shut-ins heard Sunday's sermon down the telephone, seven more than last week. The pastor has stopped asking after the valve and started thanking the operators, who say he gives a very good three minutes.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: the Jamaica Arms dinner, and who sat next to whom
columns.body: Darlings, at Saturday's dinner a certain alderman sat beside a certain utility director's wife and did not speak to her once until his minute of silence, after which she asked him for the salt. He passed it. The Society has the salt on the record, too.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Duke was given a biscuit by the Commission's clerk. Counsel objected. Overruled.

record.ear: Rain, mild. High 44. Low 36. Cutting stopped on the Sound.

lead.headline: Commission reserves decision on the Hum and the rate after a dog is heard
lead.deck: Hearing sits 4 hours 30 minutes; Dr. Rastin's survey received; the terrier Duke heard during a minute's silence at 11:16 a.m.; decision 'in February'
lead.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey reserved decision yesterday on the Astoria petition concerning the Hum and on the application of Queens Light & Power to raise its rate to 7 1/2 cents. Dr. Emil Rastin's readings at 23 places were received in evidence. At 11:16 a.m., during a minute's silence asked by Alderman Feeney, the terrier Duke was heard to howl, and Dr. Rastin's meter read 41. Company counsel's objection was noted. Mr. Roland Tisch repeated that the company produces no tone.

columns.headline: Commission's record of the minute's silence, 11:16 a.m.
columns.body: ALDERMAN FEENEY: 'One minute, Commissioner.' COMMISSIONER LACEY: 'Granted.' (Silence, 14 seconds. A dog, 9 seconds. Silence, 37 seconds.) MR. CORLISS, for the company: 'I object.' COMMISSIONER LACEY: 'To the dog, Mr. Corliss, or to the silence?' MR. CORLISS: 'To the meter.'

columns.headline: Another answering doll returned to the Arcade, from Ridgewood
columns.body: An answering doll was returned to the Vantry Arcade's toy shop yesterday by Mrs. Leopold Strub of Ridgewood, who stated it had 'said seven' at bedtime on Sunday. The proprietress played it four times and heard six. Mrs. Strub declined to give the seventh word.

columns.headline: Thaw stops ice cutting; harvest stands at 61,400 tons
columns.body: Rain and 44 degrees stopped ice cutting on the Sound at noon yesterday. The three companies have housed 61,400 tons this season, the Bowery Bay company reports. Mr. Owen Pratt says the houses are 'full enough to be quiet about it.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The toy shop has placed Mrs. Strub's doll on the back shelf beside Mrs. Voss's, both facing the wall.

speaker.ear: Rain and forty-four. The thaw is back, and it brought its umbrella.

lead.headline: Another doll learns a seventh word, and Ridgewood won't repeat the message
lead.deck: Mrs. Strub brings back a talker that spoke up at bedtime; the toy-shop lady plays it four times and gets six; the back shelf is filling up
lead.body: Mrs. Leopold Strub of Ridgewood came into the Arcade yesterday with a doll under her arm and her mouth shut tight. It had said seven words at bedtime on Sunday, she said, to her daughter. The toy-shop lady put it on the counter and played it four times. Six words each time, good as gold. Mrs. Strub pocketed her dollar seventy-five and would not say the seventh. Neither would Mrs. Voss. That makes two mothers in Queens who know a word they will not say, and no fathers.

columns.headline: The Commission reserves, and the dog is the only one who struck a clear note
columns.body: Commissioner Lacey reserved on the hum and the half cent until February, having heard four hours of men and nine seconds of terrier. The terrier was the clearer. Company counsel objected to the meter. The meter has not replied.

columns.headline: Ice men pack it in as the thaw comes back, and the houses are full
columns.body: Rain stopped the cutting on the Sound at noon, but sixty-one thousand four hundred tons are in, and Mr. Pratt says that is enough to keep Queens cold till September. He says it quietly, in case the weather hears.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What is the seventh word?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator does not know, and if she did she would not put it through. Two mothers have been asked and two mothers have declined. That is two more people than usually decline anything in Queens. Let it rest.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Two dolls on the back shelf now, both facing the wall. The toy-shop lady has started dusting them from behind.

record.ear: Clearing, colder. High 36. Low 25. Fair for the first of February.

lead.headline: Board of Elections declines to play the Riverhead transmission's 11 seconds
lead.deck: Mr. Gorman's application refused 3 to 1; the record 'sealed with the count'; bench warrant for Mr. Marchetti still outstanding
lead.body: The Board of Elections yesterday refused, by three votes to one, the application of Mr. Francis Gorman that its record of the Riverhead wire transmission of January 3 be played to counsel, the transmission having run 11 seconds longer than the Suffolk clerk's sending. Chairman Delaney said the record was 'sealed with the count, and the count is certified.' Commissioner Wallach, dissenting, said the eleven seconds 'are either something or nothing, and the Board should know which.' The bench warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Mr. Lasko's motion against the parlour record remains under advisement
columns.body: Judge Conklin has not ruled on Mr. Saul Feder's motion to exclude the Hale parlour record, and said yesterday that he will do so 'before the jury is drawn' on February 18. Detective Sergeant Edward Moran says the fur coat 'has been looked for in Corona.'

columns.headline: January's count: 412 valve failures at the Queens exchange
columns.body: The Queens exchange recorded 412 valve failures at its positions in January, against 270 in an ordinary month, the supervisor reports. The three-minute request has shortened the average call to 3 minutes 9 seconds. Newark's second salvage truck is promised for Monday.

columns.headline: Little America reports the pup Jackson 'the loudest of six'
columns.body: Commander Byrd's operator reported last night that the pup named Jackson by the Record's readers is 'thriving and the loudest of the six.' The message was played at 10 in the Record's window to 500. The ships are to sail north about February 20.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve has given notice of her motion on record No. 23 for the Society's February meeting.

speaker.ear: Clearing and colder. High 36. January hangs up tonight. February is holding.

lead.headline: Board seals the Riverhead eleven seconds, and nobody gets to listen in
lead.deck: Gorman wants to hear what the wire said in the time the clerk was silent; three commissioners say no, and one says he would rather know
lead.body: On January 3 the Riverhead returns came down the wire eleven seconds longer than the Suffolk clerk needed to send them, and Mr. Gorman has wanted to hear those eleven seconds ever since. Yesterday the Board said no, three to one. The record is sealed with the count, says Chairman Delaney, and the count is certified, and that is that. Commissioner Wallach said he would rather know. So would we. Joseph Marchetti, who might know, is still wanted, still missing, and still not writing in.

columns.headline: Lasko's judge keeps the parlour on hold till the jury is drawn
columns.body: Judge Conklin will rule on the Hale parlour before the jury is drawn on February 18, and not a day sooner. Sergeant Moran says the fur coat has been looked for in Corona. Corona says it has been looked at quite enough, thank you.

columns.headline: Party Line's admirer goes quiet, and the cat takes the call philosophically
columns.body: No tin came for Party Line this week, and the exchange has noticed. The cat has not. She sits at position 43 as before, receiving calls in her own way, which is to sit on the cords. Our page of the 12th is still with Sergeant Moran.

columns.headline: A sailor, a terrier and a sermon by telephone: January signs off
columns.body: January gave Queens a sailor in the funnies, a terrier in the witness chair, a sermon by telephone, a range of mountains, a word in Albany nobody will own, and four hundred and twelve dead valves. February has big shoes to fill. We will be listening.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The eleven seconds are sealed. Marchetti is out. The Hum is in. Good night, Queens.
